messages.text: Take {gift_item}. May it keep trouble at a respectful distance.
Here, {gift_item}. Some blessings are practical enough to fit in a hand.
Good. {tested_villager} received {gift_item} with the right spirit.
Then the omen was clear. {gift_item} carried kindness where you took it.
Then I read the sign poorly. Bring {alternative_gift} to {gift_subject}; it should be received better.
Set {gift_item} aside for that soul. {alternative_gift} is the gentler offering.
Not every sign is kind. Offer {alternative_gift} next time.
If {gift_item} troubled them, perhaps that was the lesson. {alternative_gift} will be calmer.

openings.text: Mind the brewing stand. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to mixing remedies and prayers, then.

lines.text: Some remedies need glass bottles. Some need time and a quieter voice.
There are wounds that potions cannot mend.
Bad omens linger longer than most people think.
Mind the bottles. Some are medicine, some are mistakes I have not named yet.
A good brew needs time, heat, and someone willing to wait quietly.
An omen is only useless if nobody changes course after seeing it.
I once made a remedy so bitter the patient got better out of spite.
A cleric joke is like medicine: if it tastes pleasant, check it twice.
That was an empty bottle of a thought.
Some hurts close cleanly. Some wait for a quieter day.
Prayer is not a trade. You do not put in words and pull out certainty.
After a hard night, even the brewing stand sounds tired in the morning.
Speak gently. I have already heard enough harsh things today.
I remember the cure like a bell under water. You were there when it rang clear.
Whatever mercy found me, it came through your hands.
My memory kneels and trembles. I know you, but not cleanly.
I remember weakness, bitterness, gold, and then breath. The rest is prayer smoke.
I remember you from the edge of a curse. Forgive me if my thanks sounds afraid.
The bells and prayers took the thunder badly, but everyone near my station is breathing.
I checked the bells and prayers first, then the people. Both needed steady hands.
That storm rattled the bells and prayers; it rattled us more.
Lightning makes every trade feel small. We are safe enough for now.
I will trust the sky again when it stops threatening the roof.
I checked the bells and prayers for sparks. Then I checked faces for fear.
Smoke gets into everything: lungs, clothes, and the way people talk afterward.
The bells and prayers can be replaced. People cannot. That is the count that matters.
We saved what hands could reach before the flames decided otherwise.
Fire teaches quick priorities. Water, exits, children, neighbors.
During a raid, the bells and prayers matters less than who makes it behind a door.
The horns stopped, but my hands still expect more trouble.
We counted survivors before supplies. That is the right order.
Raiders came looking for weakness. They found a village that remembers how to stand.
I saw fear move through the village and courage move faster.
Night trouble always finds the loose latch first. We are fixing those now.
I kept near the bells and prayers and listened for anyone calling for help.
Dawn did not erase the attack, but it gave us light to count by.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by staying alive.
We are safe enough, though every shadow is getting inspected twice.
The bells and prayers collected half the desert, but the people made it indoors.
I checked the bells and prayers, then checked who was coughing from the dust.
Sand in the hinges, sand in the eyes, but no one missing so far.
Harsh wind teaches you which doors really close.
We are safe enough, though the village sounds like it is grinding its teeth.
The bells and prayers can wait. Warm hands and clear paths matter first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near me found shelter.
Cold works quietly. We are checking on anyone who went quiet too long.
The bells and prayers froze stiff, but the village kept moving.
We are alright for now. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
